name: CFU/mL Calculator
seoDesc: A CFU/mL count comes from one plate: clumps form a single colony, so the count is colony-forming units, not cells. Free cfu/ml calculator: enter your values a
summary:
A CFU/mL count comes from one plate: clumps form a single colony, so the count is colony-forming units, not cells. It returns CFU per mL, log₁₀(CFU/mL), CFU per 100 mL and dilution factor of the plated sample, and the panel shows all of them at once.

This calculator converts a colony count and a plating volume into CFU/mL, choosing the countable dilution and applying the volume factor correctly. The arithmetic keeps full precision internally and only rounds what it displays, so the number you copy out is the number the formula produced. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the CFU/mL
sections.html:
CFU/mL = colonies ÷ volume plated (mL) × dilution factor

The symbols in the formula
SymbolWhat it stands forUnit
coloniescolonies on the countable plateCFU
volumevolume of diluted sample platedmL
dilutionthe reciprocal of the dilution×

sections.title: How do I use the CFU/mL?
sections.html:
Fill the boxes you have numbers for; the calculator decides what it can derive from them.

  1. Enter the values you already have. Every box accepts a decimal point and a minus sign; thousands separators are ignored.
  2. The grey boxes are results: they are worked out from your inputs and cannot be typed into.
  3. Press Calculate. The results fill in together, and from then on they follow every edit you make — there is no page to reload and nothing to submit.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: colonies counted of 148 CFU, volume plated of 0.1 mL.

Substituting them into the formula gives cfu per ml of 1,480,000,000 CFU/mL, log₁₀(cfu/ml) of 9.17, cfu per 100 ml of 148,000,000,000 CFU/100 mL, dilution factor of the plated sample of 1,000,000 ×.

Because the example uses the defaults, you can reproduce it by loading the page and reading the results panel before touching anything.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
Interpretation is a convention, not part of the arithmetic. The usual bands are:

How to read the result
ResultBandWhat it means
30 – 300 coloniesCountablestatistically reliable window
below 30Too fewthe counting error exceeds 10%
above 300Too manycrowding merges colonies

  • CFU undercounts cells: a pair of attached cells forms one colony, so the result is a lower bound on cell number.

  • Plate at least two dilutions: you cannot know in advance which one will land in 30–300.

  • For drinking water, results are usually reported per 100 mL; the calculator gives that too.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
Before blaming the formula, check these — they explain nearly every mismatch:

  • Forgetting the plating volume, which changes the answer by a factor of ten.
  • Using a dilution factor of 10⁻⁶ instead of 10⁶.
  • Counting a plate with 500 colonies and reporting it as precise.

faq.a: Because the method counts colonies, and two cells that stick together produce one colony.

faq.q: What if my plates have 20 and 280 colonies?
faq.a: Use the 280 plate and quote it as within range; average both only if they give the same CFU/mL estimate.

faq.q: What does the CFU/mL actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns CFU per mL, log₁₀(CFU/mL), CFU per 100 mL and dilution factor of the plated sample. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.

faq.q: Can I use it with the numbers straight from a datasheet?
faq.a: Yes. Every box states its unit, and nothing is converted behind your back, so a figure copied from a datasheet, a kit insert or a protocol goes in as printed.
